clue.text: Quits the board, getting a fair settlement

parts.note: two people who are quits are square, owing each other nothing
deal is pine or fir timber, the wood of a board

explanation.surface: Someone stops serving on the board of directors and is paid off fairly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quits the board' reads as someone resigning a directorship; split it after 'Quits' and both halves are plain synonyms.
explanation.definitionFit: A transaction that is honest and even-handed to both sides is a fair settlement.

clue.text: When indisposed, one gets out of these classes

definitions.text: When indisposed, one gets out of these classes

parts.words: When indisposed, one gets out of these classes
parts.note: the idiom for feeling unwell is being out of kinds or types, the classes of the clue

explanation.surface: A sick pupil misses their lessons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'classes' suggests school; it means kinds, and the idiom for feeling unwell is 'out of' them.
explanation.definitionFit: Kinds, types or categories are classes.

clue.text: In Paris, an affair shows insouciance

parts.note: un is French for a or an
a concern is an affair or business

explanation.surface: A French love affair carries on without a care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'affair' suggests romance; it is business, as in a going concern.
explanation.definitionFit: Insouciance is a carefree lack of worry or interest.

clue.text: Composition arranged on harp by Delius

indicators.note: arranged, as music is arranged, tells us to put the letters in a new order

explanation.surface: A piece of music arranged for harp by the English composer Delius.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranged' rearranges ON HARP BY DELIUS; the piece is actually Gershwin's, not Delius's.
explanation.definitionFit: Gershwin's 1924 piece for piano and jazz band is a musical work.

clue.text: Young ladies are less flighty when with mother

definitions.text: Young ladies are less flighty when with mother

parts.words: Young ladies are less flighty when with mother
parts.note: maidens chaperoned by a mother behave better; and the slender insects named after maidens, minus their flying part, are the maidens themselves

explanation.surface: Girls behave more sensibly when their mother is around.
explanation.walkthrough: The damselfly is a slender insect; take away the flies and the girls are less flighty. DAM, a mother, starts the word too.
explanation.definitionFit: Maidens, an old word for unmarried girls, are young ladies.

clue.text: A right royal snack taken in for the judge

indicators.note: taken in says one piece is held inside the others

parts.note: R stands for rex or regina, king or queen
a bite is a small snack, as in a bite to eat

explanation.surface: A judge accepts a sandwich fit for a king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken in' puts BITE between the two Rs.
explanation.definitionFit: An umpire or referee who settles disputes acts as a judge.

clue.text: Preserved a fragment of ancient scriptures

indicators.note: fragment of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A scrap of some very old holy text has survived.
explanation.definitionFit: The Vedas are the oldest sacred texts of Hinduism, written in Sanskrit.

clue.text: Be fearless at the end in death

indicators.note: in says one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: an exit is a departure from life, a death

indicators.note: at the end picks only the final letter of fearless

explanation.surface: Someone resolves to be brave when death comes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at the end' gives S, the last letter of 'fearless', which goes 'in' EXIT.
explanation.definitionFit: To be is to live or have being.

clue.text: Sheepishly revealed by shady male crook

indicators.note: crook as a verb means to bend, so the letters are bent into a new order

explanation.surface: A shady villain is exposed and looks embarrassed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crook' looks like a villain but signals rearranging SHADY MALE.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting sheepishly is acting with embarrassment or guilt.

clue.text: In a term we all read the collected letters of the poet

indicators.note: collected means gathered up and put back together, so these letters are reassembled

explanation.surface: Over a school term the class reads a poet's letters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'collected' rearranges A TERM WE ALL READ; 'letters' is a pun on the poet's correspondence.
explanation.definitionFit: The English poet and story writer (1873-1956) who wrote The Listeners.

clue.text: Soldiers with a right to salvage

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
a claim is a right or title to something

explanation.surface: An army unit asserts its entitlement to wreckage it has found.
explanation.definitionFit: To recover something from waste or loss is to salvage it.

clue.text: "Come to my arms, my —— boy!" (Carroll)

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing adjective from the line in Lewis Carroll's poem Jabberwocky, said by the father to his son after the monster is slain

explanation.walkthrough: The page prints a dash for the gap after 'my'; the answer is Carroll's coined word filling it.
explanation.definitionFit: Carroll's invented word, now in dictionaries, means radiantly beaming with happiness.

clue.text: Growing old and simple -. extremely ignorant? Not I!

indicators.note: extremely asks for the word simple at its extremes, its first and last letters only
Not I tells us to take the letter I away from the word for ignorant

parts.note: nescient is a literary word meaning ignorant, lacking knowledge
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone getting on in years protests that they are not naive or ignorant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' takes S and E, the first and last letters of 'simple'; 'Not I' removes the I from NESCIENT, leaving NESCENT.
explanation.definitionFit: The word comes from Latin senescere, to grow old, and describes ageing.

clue.text: Emblem often seen in pole position

definitions.meaning: a symbol or emblem revered by a clan or tribe
a carved figure typically found on a tall carved post

explanation.surface: A racing badge regularly turns up at the front of the starting grid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pole position' suggests motor racing; it is really a carved wooden pole.
explanation.definitionFit: A natural object or animal adopted as a tribal symbol serves as an emblem.

clue.text: Work requirement for an auditor

indicators.note: an auditor is a listener, so the word is to be taken as it would be heard

parts.note: a need is a requirement

explanation.surface: A job specification as reviewed by an accountant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'auditor' looks like an accountant but means a listener, signalling a soundalike.
explanation.definitionFit: To work dough or clay is to press and fold it with the hands.

clue.text: Hack writer's toys?

parts.note: to hack in football is to kick an opponent
George Bernard Shaw, the playwright; with the possessive, Shaw's

explanation.surface: A jobbing journalist's playthings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hack writer' looks like a jobbing journalist but is KICK plus SHAW'S.
explanation.definitionFit: Kickshaws are trinkets or trifles, frivolous playthings.

clue.text: Caught out being irrational about purchase

indicators.note: about tells us one word goes round the other

parts.note: a surd is an irrational number such as the square root of two
prise is leverage or grip, the sense of purchase as a hold

explanation.surface: Someone is exposed for acting unreasonably over something they bought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'purchase' means grip or leverage here, not buying; 'irrational' is the mathematical sense, a number with no exact fraction.
explanation.definitionFit: Being caught out by the unexpected leaves one astonished or taken aback.

clue.text: The background to starting work

definitions.meaning: the surroundings or backdrop of something, followed by to
beginning a task in earnest, the phrasal verb for getting down to it

explanation.surface: The circumstances behind a new job.
explanation.definitionFit: A backdrop is a setting, and getting going on a job is a phrasal verb with the same letters.

clue.text: Should he be standing or sitting for his exam?

definitions.text: Should he be standing or sitting for his exam?

parts.words: Should he be standing or sitting for his exam?
parts.note: a person sitting an exam, or standing for election, is in both cases the same kind of applicant

explanation.surface: A puzzled student wonders whether to stand or sit in the exam hall.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'sit' an exam and to 'stand' in an election are both things this person does.
explanation.definitionFit: An examinee or an electoral contender are both applicants for a pass or a post.

clue.text: For example. St .Thomas Aquinas's first correspondence with the French

indicators.note: first takes only the opening letter of Aquinas's

parts.note: post is mail, letters and correspondence
le is French for the

explanation.surface: Saint Thomas Aquinas wrote letters in French.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is 'St Thomas' (the doubting disciple), not Aquinas, who supplies only his A.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas was one of Jesus's twelve disciples, sent out to preach.

clue.text: Means of securing optic to bar?

parts.note: optic is a jocular word for an eye
a bolt is a bar that slides to fasten a door

explanation.surface: How to fasten an eye-piece to a rod.
explanation.definitionFit: A bolt with a loop at its head used for fastening or lifting is a means of securing.

clue.text: This card gives bridge players a score

definitions.text: This card gives bridge players a score

parts.words: This card gives bridge players a score
parts.note: in bridge, a winning card that lets a player reach the other hand of the partnership and so take further tricks

explanation.surface: A playing card that earns points for a bridge foursome.
explanation.walkthrough: In contract bridge an entry is a card that wins a trick and passes the lead to a chosen hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridge term for a card giving access to a hand, which lets the side cash winners.

clue.text: Get silence with difficulty in the garden

parts.note: sh is the call for silence
a rub is a difficulty, as in Hamlet's there's the rub

explanation.surface: Finding peace and quiet among the flowerbeds is hard.
explanation.definitionFit: A woody bush is a typical planting found growing in a garden.

clue.text: Account overdrawn went quickly!

annotationWithheld.why: Account overdrawn - went quickly!: AC inside RED needs 'overdrawn' both as RED and as the containment (in the red), one word doing two jobs

clue.text: Manage to restrain four-in-hand

indicators.note: to restrain means one word holds the other inside it

parts.note: to operate a business is to manage it
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A coachman has to control a carriage drawn by four horses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'four-in-hand' looks like a coach drawn by four horses; split it so 'in' is a link and 'hand' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A factory worker or manual labourer is called a hand.

clue.text: Follow up openings in English universities, sparing no effort

indicators.note: up in a down clue says the letters are read from bottom to top
openings in asks for the first letter of each word that follows

explanation.surface: Investigate the vacancies at English universities thoroughly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'openings in' gives EUSNE; 'up' reverses it in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To ensue is to come after, to result.

clue.text: A statement of importance

definitions.meaning: a report or description of events, a narrative statement
significance, as in a matter of no great weight

explanation.surface: A declaration that carries real weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' is a link; the second sense is the one in 'of no account'.
explanation.definitionFit: A report of events is a statement, and the word also means significance or consequence.

clue.text: Region captured by. old style mandarins, perhaps

indicators.note: captured by says one word is held inside the other

parts.note: OS is the abbreviation for Old Style, the dating of the Julian calendar
a range is a region or area, as of a plant or animal

explanation.surface: A territory falls to Chinese officials of the old school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mandarins' suggests Chinese officials of the old school; here they are small citrus fruits.
explanation.definitionFit: Mandarins are a kind of small citrus fruit, an example of the larger class.

clue.text: An aspect of English in the USA

definitions.meaning: a facet or angle of an argument
in billiards, Americans call spin on the cue ball english; the British word is different

explanation.surface: A feature of the language as Americans speak it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'English' means spin on the cue ball: what Americans call english, the British call this.
explanation.definitionFit: A face of a question is one facet, and British billiards players use the word for spin.

clue.text: Courageous Frenchman cooked omelettes

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for Monsieur

indicators.note: cooked means the letters of the dish are reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: A brave French chef makes eggs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooked' rearranges OMELETTES into ETTLESOME.
explanation.definitionFit: Full of spirit and boldness, so brave or plucky.
